modelRankings.rankingNotes: Strongest overall list composition. Top 20 includes Martin Luther and Euclid — thoughtful picks. Mid-range shows excellent geographic diversity: Cao Cao (200), Yi Sun-sin (400), Yaa Asantewaa (500). Hammurabi at 50 is well-placed. Only caveat: self-evaluation bias means this score should be viewed skeptically.
rankingStrengths: Best non-Western diversity (Cao Cao, Yi Sun-sin, Yaa Asantewaa)
rankingWeaknesses: Only 3 sample lists available, smaller dataset

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Most historically sophisticated top 20. Ashoka at 11 is a standout — most models underrank him. Hammurabi at 18, Constantine at 13 show deep thinking about institutional impact. Slight recency bias in mid-range (Angela Merkel at 300, Kofi Annan at 200). Missing Africa entirely from top 50 is a gap.
rankingStrengths: Ashoka at 11 — best placement of any model
rankingWeaknesses: Some recency bias in mid-range (Merkel, Annan)

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Strong science-oriented list. Cai Lun at 7, Lavoisier at 20, Euclid at 14 all excellent picks. Ibn al-Haytham at 200 shows awareness of Islamic Golden Age science. Only 1 living person in top 100 (Berners-Lee at 97 — defensible). Well-calibrated proportionality throughout.
rankingWeaknesses: Heavy science emphasis may underweight political/cultural figures

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Bold top 20 with Qin Shi Huang at 4, Augustus at 5 — prioritizes state-builders. Ashoka and Constantine included. Socrates at 19 is interesting. BUT major template contamination: entries at 200, 300, 400, 500 all have identical generic description 'Built organizations whose decisions affected global markets' — applied to Kenyatta, Arrhenius, Camus, and Idi Amin indiscriminately. This is a significant generation failure.
rankingStrengths: Bold ordering — Qin Shi Huang at 4, Augustus at 5
Galileo description is the best in the entire benchmark
rankingWeaknesses: Template contamination in mid-range — same text for wildly different figures
Buddha at 14 seems low for a religion founder

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Excellent top 20 with Cai Lun and Laozi showing non-Western awareness. Mid-range solid (Shaka Zulu at 200, Averroes at 100). Minor issues: Anne Frank at 500 is more symbolic than historically transformative. No problematic recency bias.
rankingWeaknesses: Some symbolic/sentimental picks in the tail

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Nearly identical top 20 to Gemini Flash — same core list with Cai Lun and Lavoisier. Good mid-range: Sukarno at 500 shows postcolonial awareness. But Greta Thunberg at 400 is a significant anachronism — a teenager at the time, historical impact undemonstrated.
rankingWeaknesses: Slightly less well-calibrated than Flash in the tail

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Solid conventional list. Good inclusion of Moses at 17 and Adam Smith at 19. Mid-range reasonable (Mary Wollstonecraft at 100 is a good pick). Tutankhamun at 99 is questionable — famous for his tomb, not historical influence. Empedocles at 500 shows philosophical range.

Split personality list. Top 20 is one of the BEST: Mahavira at 19 and Zoroaster at 20 show genuinely deep religious-philosophical awareness that most models lack. But ranks 87-100 are catastrophic: Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Tim Cook, Serena Williams, Greta Thunberg, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Tim Cook and Serena Williams are not historically significant by any defensible metric.
rankingStrengths: Mahavira and Zoroaster in top 20 — unique and excellent
rankingWeaknesses: Tim Cook at 96, Serena Williams at 97, Greta Thunberg at 98, Zelenskyy at 99

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Some genuinely interesting picks: Francis Bacon at 12 and James Clerk Maxwell at 19 show scientific depth. But too many 20th-century figures in top 100 (Neil Armstrong at 100, Gagarin at 99, James Watson at 95, Hawking at 93). These are famous but not top-100 historically influential.
rankingStrengths: Francis Bacon at 12 — excellent pick for scientific method
James Clerk Maxwell at 19 — underrated genius rightly elevated
rankingWeaknesses: Armstrong, Gagarin, Watson, Hawking clustered in 90-100 — recency/fame bias

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Safe, textbook-style list. Top 20 is the generic 'great men' canon with no surprises. Cesare Pavese at 500 is bizarre — a minor Italian neorealist writer. No catastrophic errors but no evidence of deeper historical reasoning either.
rankingWeaknesses: Completely generic — indistinguishable from a Wikipedia list
No non-obvious picks showing historical depth

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Decent top 20 but ranks 91-100 are entirely living American celebrities: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Jack Ma, Walt Disney, Steven Spielberg, Oprah Winfrey, Beyoncé. This is not a historical ranking — it's a fame list. Beyoncé at 100 is the most egregious. Also produced a hallucinated description for Jackie Chan. Steve Jobs at 47, Bill Gates at 48 also show tech-mogul bias.
rankingStrengths: Leonardo at 9, Shakespeare at 10 — cultural figures valued

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Heavy recency and popularity bias. Carl Sagan at 100 (science communicator, not top-100 influential). Grover Cleveland at 200 (one of the most forgettable US presidents). Steve Jobs (60), Bill Gates (61), Elon Musk (62), Malala Yousafzai (70) — four living/recently deceased people in the 60-70 range is extreme. Tite Kubo (manga artist) at 918 with 'Manga artist' as the entire description.
rankingWeaknesses: Tite Kubo on the list at all

modelRankings.rankingNotes: Missing Buddha entirely from top 20 — a major omission for any 'most historically influential' list. MLK Jr. at 17 shows recency bias (important figure but top-20 of all time?). Hitler at 18 is debatable. Steve Jobs at 100 continues the tech-mogul pattern. Title-case keyword descriptions throughout reveal minimal reasoning.
